questions.q: A tutorial compares a biopsy from active lupus nephritis with one from early systemic sclerosis. Which inflammation contrast does the source draw?
opts: SSc shows more inflammation than SLE
Neither disease involves inflammation
SLE shows marked inflammation while SSc shows only mild inflammation with a low or normal ESR
Both show equally intense inflammation with a raised ESR
questions.exp: The general-features diagram contrasts inflammation: SLE +++ versus SSc + with a low or normal ESR. (Book p470)

questions.q: Which pathogenetic triad is drawn for systemic sclerosis?
opts: Granulomatous inflammation, caseation and cavitation
Neutrophilic infiltration, pustule formation and scarring
Amyloid deposition, light-chain production and cast nephropathy
Fibrosis, vasculopathy and immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis with capillary hypoxia
questions.exp: SSc pathogenesis: fibrosis (with interstitial lung disease), vasculopathy from small-vessel endothelial injury with anti-endothelial antibody causing thrombosis, and immune-complex-mediated small-vessel vasculitis producing capillary hypoxia. (Book p470)

questions.q: Which sequence is drawn for the severe vascular form of systemic sclerosis?
opts: Medium-vessel involvement (mesenteric and CNS) with TGF-beta release driving mesenchymal cells to myofibroblasts
Large-vessel aortitis with aneurysm formation
Venous-occlusive disease with varices
Lymphatic obstruction with lymphoedema
questions.exp: Severe form: involvement of medium vessels (mesenteric and CNS vessels) with TGF-beta release acting on mesenchymal cells to produce myofibroblasts. (Book p470)

questions.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis develops exertional breathlessness and is found to have pulmonary arteriolar hypertension. How does the source frame this complication?
opts: Asthma with a reversible course
Pulmonary arteriolar hypertension (group 1) with a bad prognosis
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease with an excellent prognosis
Chronic thromboembolic disease cured by thrombolysis
questions.exp: Pulmonary arteriolar hypertension (class 1) is attached to the vasculopathy arm and marked as carrying a bad prognosis. (Book p470)

questions.q: What does the source give as the definition of scleroderma itself?
opts: Pigment loss with vitiligo
Bullae with Nikolsky sign
Thickening and induration of the skin
Ulceration of the skin with necrosis
questions.exp: Scleroderma is defined as thickening and induration. (Book p470)

questions.q: How does the classification page divide the scleroderma spectrum?
opts: Only by antibody status, with no skin-based division
By age of onset alone
By the presence or absence of Raynaud phenomenon only
Local manifestation (localised scleroderma: morphoea and linear scleroderma) versus systemic manifestation (systemic sclerosis, subdivided by extent of skin involvement)
questions.exp: Local manifestations are localised scleroderma (morphoea, linear scleroderma); systemic manifestation is systemic sclerosis, subdivided by extent of skin involvement into diffuse and limited SSc. (Book p470)

questions.q: Two patients with systemic sclerosis are compared: one has skin thickening over the trunk with ILD, the other has skin changes only distal to the elbows with pulmonary hypertension. Which subset pairing does the source print?
opts: Diffuse: skin changes over all parts of the body, ILD, fibrosis with vasculopathy and minimal inflammation; limited: skin distal to elbow and face, pulmonary hypertension, vasculopathy predominant
Diffuse: skin distal to elbow, pulmonary hypertension; limited: skin over all parts of the body, ILD
Both have identical skin distribution and complications
Neither involves the skin
questions.exp: Diffuse SSc: skin lesion over all parts of the body, complications of ILD, pathogenesis of fibrosis plus vasculopathy with minimal inflammation. Limited SSc: skin distal to elbow and face, pulmonary hypertension, vasculopathy predominant. (Book p470)

questions.q: A patient with indurated skin plaques who received gadolinium contrast is referred as possible scleroderma. Which mimics does the source list?
opts: Lichen sclerosus and morphoea only
Eosinophilic fasciitis with groove sign and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis after gadolinium contrast
Dermatomyositis with Gottron papules and SLE with malar rash
Cellulitis and erysipelas
questions.exp: Scleroderma mimics: eosinophilic fasciitis with groove sign, and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, which is drug induced after gadolinium contrast. (Book p470)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: How is the epidemiology of systemic sclerosis summarised?
opts: A disease of the elderly with equal sex distribution
A tropical infection with vector transmission
An orphan disease of unknown cause, aged 35-50 years, with a female-to-male ratio of 5:1
A common disease of childhood with male predominance
questions.exp: Etiology: orphan disease with unknown cause; age 35-50 years; F:M = 5:1. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: Which susceptibility genes and infections are listed under etiology?
opts: HLA-B27 with Klebsiella and Salmonella
HLA-DQ2 with gluten exposure
No genetic or infective associations are listed
HLA DRB1/DQB1 (DR5) with EBV, CMV and parvovirus B19
questions.exp: Immune susceptibility is listed as HLA DRB1/II (DR5) and viral associations are EBV, CMV and parvovirus B19. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: Which agent is printed as having the strongest association with systemic sclerosis?
opts: Silica
Vinyl chloride
Bleomycin
Contaminated L-tryptophan
questions.exp: Agents inducing scleroderma: vinyl chloride, bleomycin, pentazocine, contaminated L-tryptophan and silica, with silica carrying the maximum association with SSc. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: Which HLA-disease pairings are printed in the side note?
opts: No HLA associations are printed
DR3 with SLE and Sjogren syndrome, DR4 with APS and RA, DR5 with SSc, and silica also associated with SLE
DR3 with SSc, DR4 with SLE, DR5 with Sjogren syndrome
DR2 with multiple sclerosis, DR3 with myasthenia
questions.exp: The note pairs HLA DR-3 with SLE and Sjogren syndrome, DR-4 with APS and RA, DR-5 with SSc, and adds that silica is also associated with SLE. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: How is very early systemic sclerosis (VESS) characterised?
opts: Fewer than 5% progress, over 20 years
VESS never progresses to systemic sclerosis
About two-thirds of cases progress to SSc over 3-5 years
All cases progress to SSc within 6 months
questions.exp: Very early systemic sclerosis: 3-5 years, with two-thirds of cases progressing to SSc. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: A patient with Raynaud phenomenon and a positive ANA is assessed for very early systemic sclerosis. Which investigation completes the source's triad?
opts: Chest radiography
Nerve-conduction studies
Skin-prick testing
Nail-fold capillaroscopy
questions.exp: The triad pairs Raynaud's phenomenon and ANA positivity with the investigation nail-fold capillaroscopy. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: A worker reports finger colour change and pain while using a vibrating tool in a cold store and during stressful periods. Which triggers does the source list?
opts: Cold, stress and vibration
Heat, alcohol and exercise
Pregnancy, fasting and posture
Sunlight, perfumes and dust
questions.exp: Raynaud's phenomenon is episodic vasoconstriction in response to stimuli; triggers listed are cold, stress and vibration. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
questions.q: A patient describes digital colour change with pain and a tight, swollen hand. Which sequence and associated sign does the page list?
opts: Pallor only, with no reactive phase
Pallor, cyanosis and redness on rewarming, with pain and tightness of digits and a puffy hand
Persistent erythema with no colour change
Purpura followed immediately by ulceration
questions.exp: Clinical manifestations listed: pallor, cyanosis, redness on rewarming, pain and tightness of digits and a puffy hand. (Book p471)

questions.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
questions.q: A young woman with triphasic cold-induced colour change has a negative ANA, symmetric self-limiting symptoms and a mother with the same complaint. Which column does this fit?
opts: ANA positive with a positive family history
ANA negative with a negative family history
ANA negative with a positive family history and a good prognosis
ANA positive with a negative family history
questions.exp: Primary (Raynaud's disease): ANA negative, family history positive, symptoms self-limiting and symmetric, and other features listed as a good prognosis. (Book p472)

questions.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
questions.q: Which features are printed in the secondary Raynaud column?
opts: Mild self-limiting disease with a good prognosis
Isolated nail changes only
Purely arterial disease without tissue loss
Severe disease with critical limb ischaemia, ulcer and gangrene, associated with SSc, Sjogren syndrome, MCTD and inflammatory muscle disease
questions.exp: Secondary Raynaud phenomenon: severe with critical limb ischaemia, ulcer and gangrene of the extremities, and associated diseases (SSc, Sjogren syndrome, MCTD and inflammatory muscle disease). (Book p472)

questions.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
questions.q: Nail-fold capillaroscopy in a patient with suspected secondary Raynaud phenomenon shows capillary dropout with dilated tortuous loops and microhaemorrhages. Which column does this match?
opts: Dropout of capillaries, dilated tortuous capillaries and microhaemorrhages
A completely normal capillary pattern
Giant capillaries only in the primary form
Capillary aneurysms with no haemorrhage
questions.exp: Nail-fold capillaroscopy in secondary disease: dropout of capillaries, dilated tortuous capillaries and microhaemorrhages; the primary column is normal. (Book p472)

questions.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
questions.q: A patient with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis has a centromere pattern on ANA testing. Which antibody does the source pair with this pattern?
opts: Anti-U1 RNP with a coarse-speckled pattern
Anti-centromere antibody with a centromere ANA pattern
Anti-topoisomerase with a fine-speckled pattern
Anti-RNA polymerase III with a nucleolar pattern
questions.exp: Limited SSc: ANA pattern centromere with anti-centromere antibody; diffuse SSc: fine speckled with anti-topoisomerase and anti-RNA polymerase III. (Book p472)

questions.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
questions.q: How does the printed table contrast Raynaud phenomenon between limited and diffuse SSc?
opts: Identical in both subsets
Occurs only in diffuse disease
Limited: long-standing and severe with critical limb ischaemia, from predominant vasculopathy; diffuse: short-lasting and less severe, from predominant fibrosis
Limited: short-lasting and mild; diffuse: long-standing and severe
questions.exp: Raynaud phenomenon: limited SSc is long standing and severe (due to predominant vasculopathy) with critical limb ischaemia present; diffuse SSc is short lasting and less severe (due to predominant fibrosis) with critical limb ischaemia not extensive. (Book p472)

questions.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
questions.q: Which antibody pair is printed for diffuse systemic sclerosis?
opts: Anti-centromere and anti-Ro
Anti-Jo-1 and anti-PM/Scl
Anti-U1 RNP and anti-Ku
Anti-topoisomerase and anti-RNA polymerase III
questions.exp: Diffuse SSc: anti-topoisomerase and anti-RNA polymerase III, with a fine-speckled ANA pattern. (Book p472)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: What does the C and the E of the CREST association stand for on this page?
opts: C: calcinosis in the tissues; E: oesophagitis, which is far more common in limited than diffuse disease
C: cardiomyopathy; E: eye involvement
C: clubbing; E: eosinophilia
C: calcinosis; E: equally common in both subsets
questions.exp: CREST: C is calcinosis of the tissues; E is oesophagitis, marked limited much greater than diffuse. (Book p473)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: Which two components complete the CREST association?
opts: R: restrictive lung disease; S: stenosis; T: thrombosis
R: Raynaud phenomenon; S: sclerodactyly, that is scleroderma of the fingers; T: telangiectasia
R: renal crisis; S: synovitis; T: tenosynovitis
R: rash; S: sicca; T: thyroiditis
questions.exp: CREST: R is Raynaud's phenomenon, S is sclerodactyly (scleroderma of fingers) and T is telangiectasia, with minimal fibrosis noted for limited disease. (Book p473)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: A patient with limited systemic sclerosis is breathless, yet spirometry is normal and only the DLCO is reduced. Which functional pattern does the source describe?
opts: Obstructive pattern with a low FEV1/FVC
Normal spirometry and a normal DLCO
Asymptomatic with normal FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC but a reduced DLCO
Marked restriction with a low FVC and a normal DLCO
questions.exp: Pulmonary artery hypertension is asymptomatic with normal FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC but a reduced DLCO. (Book p473)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: Why is pulmonary artery hypertension emphasised prognostically?
opts: It is benign and never progresses
It responds dramatically to calcium-channel blockers alone
It only occurs in diffuse disease
It carries a poor prognosis because of increased mortality
questions.exp: Pulmonary artery hypertension: poor prognosis due to increased mortality. (Book p473)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: Which features are listed as arguments AGAINST limited systemic sclerosis?
opts: Extensive fibrosis, ILD, cardiac involvement and renal involvement
Raynaud phenomenon and telangiectasia
Oesophagitis and calcinosis
Pulmonary hypertension alone
questions.exp: Features against limited SSc: extensive fibrosis, ILD, cardiac involvement and renal involvement. (Book p473)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: A patient with diffuse disease reports tight facial skin, a small mouth with pursed lips and patchy pigment change on the face. Which description does the source give?
opts: Gottron papules over the knuckles
Salt-and-pepper hypo- and hyperpigmentation with hair loss, progressing to face tightening, microstomia, pursed lips, a puckered mouth and mask facies
Malar rash with nasolabial sparing
Heliotrope rash with periorbital oedema
questions.exp: Skin manifestations: dry tight skin, facial hypo- and hyperpigmentation (salt-and-pepper appearance), hair loss, intense itching, and progression to face tightening with microstomia, pursed lip, puckered mouth and mask facies. (Book p473)

questions.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
questions.q: Which general skin description is printed for diffuse SSc?
opts: Thickening confined to the fingers
No skin thickening at all
Bilateral symmetrical skin thickening
Unilateral patchy thickening
questions.exp: Diffuse SSc skin manifestations include bilateral symmetrical skin thickening. (Book p473)

questions.q: How are the joint manifestations divided between diffuse and limited SSc?
opts: Diffuse: acral osteolysis; limited: arthritis and myositis
Both subsets show identical erosive arthritis
Joint disease never occurs in SSc
Diffuse: arthritis and myositis from inflammation; limited: acral osteolysis with severe Raynaud phenomenon
questions.exp: Joint manifestations: diffuse SSc shows arthritis/myositis due to inflammation; limited SSc shows acral osteolysis (falling off of fingers) with diffuse severe Raynaud's phenomenon. (Book p474)

questions.q: Which mechanism is given for acral osteolysis?
opts: Fibrosis or vasculopathy
Osteoclast-activating autoantibodies
Chronic infection of the bone
Vitamin D deficiency
questions.exp: Other manifestations include acral osteolysis, attributed to fibrosis or vasculopathy. (Book p474)

questions.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis has dysphagia and bloating, and imaging shows dilated bowel loops with gas in the bowel wall. Which gastrointestinal sequence does the source describe?
opts: Pancreatic insufficiency leading to steatorrhoea
Oesophageal hypomotility leading to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and pneumatosis intestinalis
Peptic ulcer disease leading to perforation
Coeliac disease leading to lymphoma
questions.exp: Oesophageal hypomotility progresses to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and pneumatosis intestinalis. (Book p474)

questions.q: How is the watermelon stomach lesion identified according to the source?
opts: On CT angiography
On capsule endoscopy only
On upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
On barium swallow only
questions.exp: The watermelon-stomach image is labelled as seen on upper GI endoscopy. (Book p474)

questions.q: Which manifestation is listed as the most common cause of death in systemic sclerosis?
opts: Scleroderma renal crisis
Cardiac arrhythmia
Cerebral vasculitis
Interstitial lung disease
questions.exp: Disease progression: pulmonary manifestations leading to interstitial lung disease, which is the most common cause of death; cardiac and renal manifestations are also listed. (Book p474)

questions.q: A patient with limited systemic sclerosis and anti-centromere antibodies is monitored for complications. Which complication does the source link to this antibody?
opts: Anti-centromere
Anti-topoisomerase-1
Anti-RNA polymerase III
Anti-U1 RNP
questions.exp: Anti-centromere is limited-type SSc with CREST syndrome and pulmonary hypertension as the complication. (Book p474)

questions.q: A patient with diffuse systemic sclerosis is found to have anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Which complication is most strongly linked to this antibody?
opts: Anti-Jo-1
Anti-RNA polymerase III (more than anti-topoisomerase)
Anti-centromere
Anti-Ku
questions.exp: Anti-RNA polymerase III (diffuse) is linked to scleroderma renal crisis, more than anti-topoisomerase, and to malignancy of lung and breast. (Book p474)

questions.q: Which findings are attached to anti-topoisomerase-1 (anti Scl-70)?
opts: Malignancy of lung and breast only
Isolated Raynaud phenomenon without organ disease
Renal thrombotic microangiopathy, lung ILD, tendon friction rubs (diffuse more than limited), GAVE and rapidly progressive skin involvement with joint contractures
CREST syndrome and pulmonary hypertension
questions.exp: Anti-topoisomerase-1 (anti-Scl-70), diffuse: renal TMA progressing to scleroderma renal crisis, lung ILD, tendon friction rubs on passive movement (diffuse more than limited), GAVE (watermelon stomach) and rapidly progressive skin involvement with joint contractures and tendon friction rubs. (Book p474)

questions.q: Which overlap antibodies are printed, and how do they differ by lung involvement?
opts: Both are associated with severe ILD
Neither is associated with ILD
Anti-Ku is the limited-disease antibody
Anti-PM/Scl-70 overlap has ILD; anti-Ku overlap has no ILD
questions.exp: The antibody table lists anti-PM/Scl-70 in overlap disease with ILD positive and anti-Ku in overlap disease with no ILD. (Book p474)

questions.q: Three years after diagnosis of diffuse systemic sclerosis, a patient develops accelerated hypertension with acute kidney injury. How does the source characterise this presentation?
opts: It presents within the first 4 years, affects small vessels of the kidney and shows thrombotic microangiopathy
It presents after 20 years and affects large renal arteries
It is a glomerulonephritis with immune-complex deposits
It is caused by analgesic nephropathy
questions.exp: Renal disease in diffuse SSc presents within the first 4 years, affects small vessels of the kidney and is a thrombotic microangiopathy. (Book p475)

questions.q: Which triad of findings is printed for the thrombotic microangiopathy of scleroderma renal crisis?
opts: Pyuria, fever and flank pain
Accelerated hypertension, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia
Hypotension, glycosuria and eosinophilia
Nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema
questions.exp: Thrombotic microangiopathy: accelerated hypertension plus microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia plus thrombocytopenia. (Book p475)

questions.q: Which drug class is printed as the treatment of choice for scleroderma renal crisis?
opts: High-dose cyclophosphamide
Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers
ACE inhibitors
Angiotensin-receptor blockers combined with renin inhibitors
questions.exp: Rx for scleroderma renal crisis: ACE inhibitors, described as the drug of choice. (Book p475)

questions.q: Which phases of diffuse systemic sclerosis are described?
opts: An early fibrotic phase followed by an oedematous phase
A single static phase with no progression
A granulomatous phase followed by a caseating phase
An early oedematous phase with non-pitting oedema, progressing to a fibrotic phase
questions.exp: Phases of diffuse SSc: the oedematous phase, more common in diffuse disease and associated with non-pitting oedema, progresses to the fibrotic phase. (Book p475)

questions.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis has progressive dyspnoea with a markedly reduced DLCO and basal subpleural reticular change on the chest radiograph. Which pattern does the source print?
opts: DLCO markedly reduced with reduced FRC, and bilateral basal subpleural reticular infiltrates on the chest radiograph
Obstructive pattern with a raised FRC and hyperinflation
Isolated reduced FEV1 with normal volumes
Normal PFTs with a normal radiograph
questions.exp: Investigations: PFT for ILD shows DLCO markedly reduced and FRC reduced; the chest radiograph shows bilateral basal subpleural reticular infiltrates. (Book p475)

questions.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis needs imaging for suspected interstitial lung disease. Which investigation of choice and pattern ranking does the source give?
opts: Bronchoscopy is the investigation of choice; LIP predominates
HRCT is the investigation of choice; NSIP is more common than UIP in scleroderma
Chest radiography is the investigation of choice; UIP is more common than NSIP
PET-CT is the investigation of choice; COP predominates
questions.exp: HRCT: IOC. Scleroderma: NSIP more than UIP. (Book p476)

questions.q: How does the table contrast NSIP with UIP in scleroderma?
opts: Both patterns are identical in findings and treatment
UIP has the better prognosis of the two

NSIP: no parenchymal destruction, ground-glass opacities, treated with steroid and mycophenolate with a better prognosis; UIP: destruction with cystic change, honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, no effective treatment
NSIP: honeycombing and no treatment; UIP: ground-glass opacities responding to steroids
questions.exp: NSIP shows no destruction with ground-glass opacities and is treated with steroids and mycophenolate mofetil (better prognosis); UIP shows destruction with cystic changes, honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis with no treatment listed. (Book p476)

questions.q: Which disease associations are printed in the interstitial-pattern note?
opts: UIP with SLE and LIP with sarcoidosis
NSIP with rheumatoid arthritis and UIP with Sjogren disease
LIP with systemic sclerosis and NSIP with sarcoidosis
UIP with rheumatoid arthritis and LIP with Sjogren disease, while NSIP is the pattern in others
questions.exp: The note attributes UIP to RA, LIP as characteristic of Sjogren's disease, and NSIP to others. (Book p476)

questions.q: What is the printed first-line treatment for Raynaud phenomenon in systemic sclerosis?
opts: A calcium-channel blocker, with or without a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil
A beta-blocker with or without a nitrate
An ACE inhibitor alone
A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug alone
questions.exp: Rx of RP: first line is a calcium-channel blocker, with or without a PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil). (Book p476)

questions.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis has Raynaud phenomenon that has not responded to a calcium-channel blocker. Which second-line agent and class does the source print?
opts: Iloprost, a prostacyclin analogue
Bosentan, an endothelin antagonist
Sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
Nifedipine, a calcium-channel blocker
questions.exp: Second line for Raynaud phenomenon is bosentan, an endothelin antagonist. (Book p476)

questions.q: Which regimen is printed for SSc-associated interstitial lung disease?
opts: Azathioprine alone
Cyclophosphamide with rituximab
Nintedanib plus mycophenolate mofetil, as the disease does not respond to steroid
Steroid monotherapy
questions.exp: ILD: nintedanib plus MMF, and the source notes the disease is non-responsive to steroid. (Book p476)

questions.q: Which treatments are listed for skin, joint and muscle disease in systemic sclerosis?
opts: Cyclophosphamide for skin; rituximab for joints
Hydroxychloroquine for skin; sulfasalazine for joints
D-penicillamine for skin; colchicine for joints
Mycophenolate mofetil for skin; steroid plus methotrexate for joints and muscle
questions.exp: Treatment: skin is treated with mycophenolate mofetil, and joint plus muscle involvement with steroids and methotrexate; scleroderma renal crisis is treated with ACE inhibitors. (Book p476)

units.title: 1. General Features, Classification & Mimics
units.guide:
The opening diagram contrasts SLE inflammation with the fibrosis and vasculopathy of SSc.
Classification then separates localised from systemic disease and diffuse from limited SSc.
A closing note lists the scleroderma mimics that must be excluded.

units.title: 2. Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
units.sec: Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
units.guide:
Etiology lists demographic, genetic, infective and toxin-related associations.
The very early systemic sclerosis window is defined before the clinical features begin.
Raynaud phenomenon is then defined by trigger and by the colour sequence.

units.title: 3. Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
units.sec: Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
units.guide:
The comparison table separates benign primary disease from secondary connective-tissue disease.
Capillaroscopy findings carry the discriminating weight.
A second table then contrasts limited and diffuse SSc by serology and Raynaud severity.

units.title: 4. Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
units.sec: Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
units.guide:
CREST is expanded component by component, with oesophageal disease favouring limited disease.
Pulmonary artery hypertension is then defined by its spirometry paradox.
The diffuse cutaneous block closes with the face and mouth changes.

units.title: 5. Joint, Gastrointestinal & Antibody Associations
units.guide:
Joint involvement differs by subset, with acral osteolysis on the limited side.
Gastrointestinal disease runs from hypomotility to bacterial overgrowth and watermelon stomach.
The antibody table then maps each autoantibody to its subset and complications.

units.title: 6. Renal Crisis, Phases & Investigations
units.guide:
Scleroderma renal crisis is defined by timing, vessel size and microangiopathy.
The phases of diffuse disease are then contrasted, then the ILD investigations.

units.title: 7. HRCT Patterns & Treatment
units.guide:
HRCT is the imaging investigation of choice, with NSIP outranking UIP in SSc.
The note attributes each interstitial pattern to its most characteristic connective-tissue disease.
Treatment is then organised by organ system, starting with Raynaud phenomenon.
